analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent federal board to investigate police killings, shootings, and severe injuries in custody.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in committee after its May 2025 referral, with no hearing, vote, or further action, and support from only 5 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a new independent federal agency, much like the National Transportation Safety Board model it borrows from, to investigate every death in police custody, officer-involved shooting, and use of force causing severe injury in custody nationwide. The board would have subpoena power, could order autopsies and test weapons, would publish detailed findings including demographics of victims and officers, and could recommend reforms that recipients must answer in writing within 90 days. States and police departments that take federal law enforcement grants could lose 1 to 10 percent of that money if they refuse to let board findings be used in court cases. The board's own power is mostly investigative and advisory; actual discipline of officers and prosecution would still be left to local authorities and the Justice Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of people killed or seriously injured by police, who would get an independent federal investigation instead of relying solely on the department involved, plus a designated point of contact for counseling and support. Communities that want consistent, public data on who is harmed by police and what happened in each case.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families of people harmed by police

how_it_helps.text: The board would investigate deaths in police custody, officer-involved shootings, and uses of force causing severe bodily injury, and publish findings including victim and officer demographics and the circumstances of each incident [S2].
The board would have subpoena power, could order autopsies, and could test and preserve any weapon involved, with results made promptly available [S2].
Families of people killed or seriously injured would be briefed before public briefings, informed of hearings, and connected to mental health and counseling services [S2].

Any department or state receiving reform recommendations would have to respond in writing within 90 days, and the Justice Department could use a failure to act on recommendations as evidence for a pattern-or-practice investigation [S2].

States or localities taking federal law enforcement grant money could lose 1 to 10 percent of it if they do not change their laws to make board findings admissible in criminal and civil cases involving police violence [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund an open-ended appropriation for a new agency with staff in every state. Police departments and local governments, which would lose control over investigating their own use-of-force incidents and could lose federal grant money for noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in appropriations and requires at least one full-time investigator in every state far from a regional office, creating a costly new federal agency with no funding estimate [S2].

The board's power is largely advisory: it cannot fire, discipline, arrest, or prosecute officers, and its reports generally cannot be used as evidence in civil damage lawsuits, so victims' wrongful-death cases gain little from it directly [S2].

Board findings would only be admissible in court, and shown to juries, in states that pass laws to conform, leaving the board's practical impact on prosecutions dependent on state legislatures it does not control [S2].
It overlaps with existing federal and state mechanisms, including Justice Department pattern-or-practice investigations and state-level review, which opponents would call duplicative [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The real value is information and pressure: independent fact-finding, public data, mandatory written responses to recommendations, and a funding penalty for states that refuse to use the findings. That is meaningful for a problem where departments typically investigate themselves, but an honest supporter has to acknowledge that the board could not itself remove a bad officer or force a prosecution, the court-admissibility improvements hinge on state cooperation, the cost is uncapped, and some protections for victims are undercut by the ban on using board reports in civil damage suits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Transportation committees in May 2025 and has seen no hearing, markup, vote, or other action since, while the 119th Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on May 29, 2025, with Reps. Bennie Thompson, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jim McGovern as original cosponsors [S2].
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, for provisions in its jurisdiction, the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no vote [S4].
Five members, all Democrats, had cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, police departments and their unions benefit from the status quo, which leaves departments and their state and local overseers as the main investigators of their own use-of-force incidents. No one in the general public gains from a bill sitting dormant, though it could still move before the Congress ends.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred, but all six supporters on the record are Democrats and none of the 223 House Republicans signed on, so the bill splits along party lines.

industries.note: The bill takes away the current arrangement in which departments largely control the investigation of their own shootings and custody deaths, replacing it with an independent federal investigator whose findings must be answered in writing and could be shown to juries. Unions and departments have historically fought outside investigative authority of this kind, though no organized opposition appears in this record.

Governments taking Byrne JAG grant money would have to change their laws to admit board findings in court or risk losing 1 to 10 percent of that funding, but they also gain detailed federal investigation reports in serious incidents. Their interest in holding onto grant money runs against the public's interest in usable findings.
The bill requires designating an independent nonprofit to coordinate mental health and counseling for victims and families after police violence, a new funded role for such organizations.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority, no Republican cosponsors, and the bill stuck without a hearing in Judiciary and Transportation, the realistic path is that it dies at the end of this Congress without a vote. It could be reintroduced in a future Congress if control of the House changes.
